etymology: Leisure (Old French leisir, permission, free time) + suit. The leisure suit — a matching shirt-jacket and trousers, usually polyester double-knit in pastel or earth tones, worn with an open-collared shirt and often a wide collar spread over the lapels — was a men’s fashion of the early-to-late 1970s, peaking around 1975–77 alongside disco. It promised the ease of casual clothes with the look of a suit, and within a few years became the decade’s most-mocked garment.
biblical_def: The leisure suit was the 1970s man’s idea of relaxed elegance: a powder-blue polyester jacket and slacks, no tie, collar spread wide, a gold chain at the neck. It promised that a man could look dressed up while living as if every day were Saturday. The Christian observation: the garment is a joke now, but the idea behind it — a life of leisure as the goal — is not, and Scripture speaks to it carefully. Leisure is a gift. The Lord Jesus Himself, when His disciples "had no leisure so much as to eat," said, "Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while" (Mar 6:31). The Preacher commends enjoying the fruit of labor as "from the hand of God" (Ecc 2:24), and "The sleep of a labouring man is sweet" (Ecc 5:12). But in Scripture leisure is the rest that follows work, not a lifestyle that replaces it, and the Sabbath rhythm of six and one holds the two together. The 1970s sold the dream of the man permanently off duty, and the leisure suit was its uniform. A second lesson hides in how quickly it became ridiculous: "the fashion of this world passeth away" (1Co 7:31). What looked sharp in 1976 looked absurd by 1980. A grandparent’s photo album is the best sermon on that verse ever preached.
webster_summary: 1970s men’s fashion (peak 1975–77): a polyester shirt-jacket and slacks for dressed-up ease — the uniform of a leisure lifestyle Scripture answers with rest after labor (Mar 6:31) and the reminder that the fashion of this world passeth away (1Co 7:31).
webster_full: LEISURE SUIT, n. (1970s; Boomer era) A man’s casual suit of matching shirt-style jacket and trousers, usually of polyester double-knit, worn without a tie; emblematic of 1970s fashion.

Webster (1828) — LEISURE, noun lezh’ur or lee’zhur. 1. Freedom from occupation or business; vacant time; time free from employment. The desire of leisure is much more natural than of business and care. I shall leave with him that rebuke to be considered at his leisure 2. Convenience of time. He sigh’d, and had no leisure more to say. [ Not used .]
Decode for families: if Grandpa owned one, there is a photo. Find it.
scriptures: Mar 6:31
And he said unto them, Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while: for there were many coming and going, and they had no leisure so much as to eat.
Ecc 2:24
There is nothing better for a man, than that he should eat and drink, and that he should make his soul enjoy good in his labour. This also I saw, that it was from the hand of God.
Ecc 5:12
The sleep of a labouring man is sweet, whether he eat little or much: but the abundance of the rich will not suffer him to sleep.
And they that use this world, as not abusing it: for the fashion of this world passeth away.
corruption_summary: The leisure suit dressed up the dream of a life permanently off duty; Scripture gives leisure as rest after labor within God’s rhythm, and shows in every faded fashion that this world’s fashion passeth away.
corruption_paragraphs: The 1970s were the first decade in which a large middle class could imagine leisure as an identity: the weekend home, the boat, the golf course, early retirement. The leisure suit expressed it in fabric. Scripture has no quarrel with rest, but it does not let rest become the purpose of life. Work is a calling given before the fall, and rest is its crown, not its replacement. A man who lives for the weekend has inverted the order of creation.

The comedy of the leisure suit also preaches. In 1976 it was the height of style; by 1980 it was a punchline; today it is a costume. Paul’s word that "the fashion of this world passeth away" (1Co 7:31) uses the very word schēma, outward form, that describes a fashion. A Christian can enjoy clothes without trusting them to define him — and can laugh at his own old photos as a lesson in eternity.
roots_summary: Latin licere (to be permitted) → Old French leisir → English leisure + Old French siute (a set, a following) → suit → 1970s leisure suit.
roots_lines: Latin licere — to be allowed; Old French leisir — free time
Old French siute — a following, a set → English suit of clothes
Early 1970s: polyester double-knit makes the leisure suit cheap and wrinkle-free
c. 1975–77: peak popularity alongside disco
Greek schēma — outward form, fashion (1Co 7:31)
usage: "Grandpa wore a baby-blue leisure suit to his brother’s wedding in 1976. Grandma kept the photo for leverage."
Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while (Mar 6:31).
The fashion of this world passeth away (1Co 7:31).

etymology: The fashion trade paper Women’s Wear Daily is credited with naming hot pants in late 1970 for very short, tight shorts worn by women as fashion rather than sportswear, often with boots or tights; they were a craze of 1971 (James Brown’s "Hot Pants," 1971). Pants is short for pantaloons (from Pantalone, the Venetian stock character of the commedia dell’arte), and hot carried its slang sense of sexy. An older vulgar sense of hot pants — sexual desire — existed alongside.
biblical_def: Hot pants were the very short, tight shorts that became a women’s fashion craze in 1971 — on city streets, on airline stewardesses, on television dancers. The name said frankly what they were for. The Christian observation: Scripture’s first word about clothing is about covering. After the fall, "they knew that they were naked; and they sewed fig leaves together, and made themselves aprons" (Gen 3:7), and then "Unto Adam also and to his wife did the LORD God make coats of skins, and clothed them" (Gen 3:21). God improved on the fig leaf; He covered more, not less. The prophet describes the humiliation of proud Babylon in terms of exposure: "make bare the leg, uncover the thigh ... Thy nakedness shall be uncovered, yea, thy shame shall be seen" (Isa 47:2–3). What God treats as the shame of judgment, the 1971 fashion page marketed as liberation. Paul’s counsel is positive, not merely negative: "that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety" (1Ti 2:9), and Peter points to "the hidden man of the heart" as the true ornament (1Pe 3:4). This is not a rule about inches handed down by grumpy men; it is a vision of dignity. A father tells his daughter: you are worth covering, the way God covered Eve. He tells his son: the fashion that uncovers her is not a gift to you but a test, and you must pass it.
webster_summary: 1971 fashion craze (named by Women’s Wear Daily, 1970) for very short, tight women’s shorts — an uncovering Scripture associates with shame (Isa 47:2–3), set against the God who clothed Adam and Eve (Gen 3:21) and the call to modest apparel (1Ti 2:9).
webster_full: HOT PANTS, n. pl. (Boomer era, 1970–71) Very short, close-fitting shorts worn by women as fashion. Older vulgar sense: sexual desire ("to have hot pants for someone").

Webster (1828) — PANTALOON, noun 1. A garment for males in which breeches and stockings are in a piece; a species of close long trowsers extending to the heels. 2. A character in the Italian comedy, and a buffoon in pantomimes; so called from his close dress.
Decode for families: the 1971 hot pants are the ancestors of every later fashion that sold exposure as freedom.
scriptures: Gen 3:7
And the eyes of them both were opened, and they knew that they were naked; and they sewed fig leaves together, and made themselves aprons.
Gen 3:21
Unto Adam also and to his wife did the LORD God make coats of skins, and clothed them.
Isa 47:2
Take the millstones, and grind meal: uncover thy locks, make bare the leg, uncover the thigh, pass over the rivers.
Isa 47:3
Thy nakedness shall be uncovered, yea, thy shame shall be seen: I will take vengeance, and I will not meet thee as a man.
In like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array;
But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.
corruption_summary: Hot pants sold exposure as liberation and named the garment for the desire it provoked; Scripture treats uncovering as shame and covering as God’s gift of dignity.
corruption_paragraphs: Fashion historians describe hot pants as an act of liberation — women claiming the right to wear what they liked. But the name gives the game away. The garment was designed and named for the eyes of men, and the industry that sold it profited from women’s bodies whether or not the women profited. The sexual revolution often worked that way: it promised freedom and delivered display. Scripture’s word for that display is in Isa 47 and Pro 7:10, and it is not a compliment.

The positive vision is better than the prohibition. God clothed the first couple Himself (Gen 3:21), with garments that cost an animal’s life — the first hint that covering comes by sacrifice. The modest apparel of 1Ti 2:9 is not a burden but a dignity, and the hidden man of the heart (1Pe 3:4) is the beauty that does not need to be uncovered to be seen.
roots_summary: Pantalone (Venetian commedia character) → French pantalon → English pantaloons → American pants + slang hot (sexy) → hot pants (Women’s Wear Daily, 1970).
roots_lines: Italian Pantalone — the old Venetian merchant of the commedia dell’arte, in tight trousers
French pantalon → English pantaloons (1828) → American pants (19th c.)
Slang hot — sexually attractive or aroused (early 20th c.)
Late 1970: Women’s Wear Daily names the fashion hot pants
1971: the craze peaks; James Brown, "Hot Pants"
usage: "Grandma says her father saw her in hot pants once in 1971 and she never wore them again."
Unto Adam also and to his wife did the LORD God make coats of skins, and clothed them (Gen 3:21).
Modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety (1Ti 2:9).

etymology: Invented in 1975 by Josh Reynolds and Maris Ambats in New York: a ring set with a clear stone over a layer of thermochromic liquid crystals that change color with temperature, sold with a chart claiming that each color reveals the wearer’s mood (blue for calm or happy, black for stressed, and so on). Millions were sold in 1975–76; the fad faded by the end of the decade and has returned periodically as a nostalgia item.
biblical_def: A mood ring was a 1975 novelty: a ring whose stone changed color with the warmth of your finger, supposedly showing whether you were calm, happy, nervous, or angry. Millions of teenagers checked their rings to find out how they felt, and checked their dates’ rings to find out how they felt about them. The Christian observation: the fad is funny, but it reveals a deep wish — to have the heart made readable — and a deep confusion about where to look. A mood ring reads skin temperature, not the soul. Scripture says the heart cannot be read so easily, even by its owner: "The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?" (Jer 17:9). Only God can: "Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts" (Psa 139:23). "The LORD looketh on the heart" (1Sa 16:7). The mood ring also reflects the 1970s turn toward feelings as the truest thing about a person — the mood as the self. Scripture asks the believer to rule his moods rather than be ruled by them: "He that hath no rule over his own spirit is like a city that is broken down, and without walls" (Pro 25:28), and "Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life" (Pro 4:23). A child can enjoy a mood ring as a toy. But his parents can teach him that God knows his heart better than any stone, and that he is more than the color of his feelings today.
webster_summary: 1975 novelty ring (Reynolds and Ambats) whose heat-sensitive stone changed color, supposedly revealing the wearer’s mood — a wish to read the heart that Scripture reserves to God (Jer 17:9; Psa 139:23), with a call to rule one’s spirit (Pro 25:28).
webster_full: MOOD RING, n. (1975; Boomer era fad) A ring with a stone containing thermochromic liquid crystals that change color with temperature, popularly claimed to indicate the wearer’s emotional state.

Webster (1828) — MOOD, noun [Latin animus.] 1. Temper of mind; temporary state of the mind in regard to passion or feeling; humor; as a melancholy mood; an angry mood; a suppliant mood 2. Anger; heat of temper. [In this sense Little Used , unless qualified by an adjective.]
Decode for families: today’s apps that track your mood are the mood ring with a subscription.
scriptures: Jer 17:9
The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?
Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts:

But the LORD said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.
He that hath no rule over his own spirit is like a city that is broken down, and without walls.
Pro 4:23
Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life.
corruption_summary: The mood ring promised to make the heart readable and treated mood as the self; Scripture says only God searches the heart and calls the believer to rule his spirit, not to be ruled by it.
corruption_paragraphs: The mood ring was harmless as a toy, but it belonged to a decade that was learning to treat feelings as the deepest truth about a person. "How do you feel about it?" replaced "Is it right?" as the moral question, and the mood ring was the cheerful jewelry of that shift. Two generations later, we have apps that track moods and a culture that treats every feeling as a fact to be affirmed. Scripture’s Jer 17:9 is the corrective: the heart is not a reliable narrator.

There is also a gentle superstition in the fad: a stone that tells you something about yourself. Many teenagers half-believed it. The Christian learns to look elsewhere — to the God who searches hearts (Psa 139:23) and to His Word, which is "a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart." That is a mirror worth checking.
roots_summary: Old English mód (mind, spirit, temper) + ring → 1975 mood ring (thermochromic liquid crystal novelty).
roots_lines: Old English mód — mind, heart, spirit; courage; temper
Old English hring — a ring, a circle
1975: Josh Reynolds and Maris Ambats market the mood ring
1975–76: millions sold; a Boomer-era fad alongside the pet rock
Hebrew lev — heart, the inner self (Jer 17:9; Pro 4:23)
usage: "Grandma’s mood ring turned black at her own wedding. She says it was the August heat."
Search me, O God, and know my heart (Psa 139:23).
Keep thy heart with all diligence (Pro 4:23).

etymology: Created in 1975 by Gary Dahl, a California advertising man, as a joke: an ordinary smooth stone sold in a cardboard pet carrier with straw bedding and a tongue-in-cheek manual, The Care and Training of Your Pet Rock. Priced at $3.95, it sold more than a million units in the months before Christmas 1975 and made Dahl a millionaire, then vanished almost as quickly. The phrase became shorthand for any absurd fad.
biblical_def: The pet rock was the great joke-fad of 1975: an ordinary stone in a box, with a manual explaining how to teach it to sit and stay. Americans bought more than a million of them. Everyone knew it was a joke; that was the joke. The Christian observation: the pet rock is the funniest commentary on idolatry ever sold at a department store. The prophets had been making the same joke for three thousand years. Isaiah describes the man who cuts down a tree, cooks his dinner over half of it, and of the rest "maketh a god, even his graven image: he falleth down unto it, and worshippeth it, and prayeth unto it, and saith, Deliver me; for thou art my god" (Isa 44:17). Habakkuk: "Woe unto him that saith to the wood, Awake; to the dumb stone, Arise, it shall teach!" (Hab 2:19). The Psalmist on idols: "They have mouths, but they speak not: eyes have they, but they see not" (Psa 115:5). The pet rock buyer laughed because he knew the rock could not hear. The idolater does not laugh, but his rock is just as deaf. Scripture’s answer is a different Rock entirely: "The LORD is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer" (Psa 18:2); "For their rock is not as our Rock" (Deu 32:31); "that Rock was Christ" (1Co 10:4). A grandparent can tell the story of the pet rock and ask a grandchild the question the prophets asked: what are you trusting that cannot hear you?
webster_summary: 1975 novelty (Gary Dahl): an ordinary stone sold as a pet with a training manual — the prophets’ own joke about idols (Isa 44:17; Hab 2:19), and a foil for the true Rock, which is Christ (1Co 10:4).
webster_full: PET ROCK, n. (1975; Boomer era fad) A smooth stone marketed as a pet, sold in a carrying box with a humorous care-and-training manual; hence any absurd, short-lived fad.
Webster (1828) — PET, noun [formerly peat. Latin peto.] 1. A cade lamb; a lamb brought up by hand. 2. A fondling; any little animal fondled and indulged.
Decode for families: the pet rock was a self-aware joke; many later fads are the same joke without the self-awareness.
scriptures: And the residue thereof he maketh a god, even his graven image: he falleth down unto it, and worshippeth it, and prayeth unto it, and saith, Deliver me; for thou art my god.
Hab 2:19
Woe unto him that saith to the wood, Awake; to the dumb stone, Arise, it shall teach! Behold, it is laid over with gold and silver, and there is no breath at all in the midst of it.
They have mouths, but they speak not: eyes have they, but they see not:
For their rock is not as our Rock, even our enemies themselves being judges.
And did all drink the same spiritual drink: for they drank of that spiritual Rock that followed them: and that Rock was Christ.
Psa 18:2
The LORD is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer; my God, my strength, in whom I will trust; my buckler, and the horn of my salvation, and my high tower.
corruption_summary: A harmless joke fad that doubles as the prophets’ satire of idolatry; Scripture laughs at the deaf stone and points to the Rock that hears, which is Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: There is nothing wicked in buying a joke for $3.95. The pet rock was a parody of consumer culture, and its buyers were in on it. But it is worth noticing how easily a joke and a religion sit side by side. People who laughed at the pet rock also bought crystals for healing, wore amulets for luck, and consulted horoscopes — trusting deaf things with real hopes. The prophets would see no difference between the pet rock and the crystal except that the pet rock was honest about itself.

Scripture’s Rock is the opposite of a pet. You do not train Him; He trains you. You do not carry Him in a box; He carries you. "The LORD is my rock, and my fortress" (Psa 18:2), and Paul identifies that Rock with Christ, who followed Israel through the wilderness and gave them water (1Co 10:4). A family can keep a pet rock on the shelf as a reminder of the difference.
roots_summary: Old English pet (?)/Scots pet (a tame animal) + Old French roque (rock) → 1975 Pet Rock (Gary Dahl).
roots_lines: Pet — a tame animal kept for companionship; a lamb brought up by hand (1828)
Old French roque, Medieval Latin rocca — rock
April 1975: Gary Dahl conceives the Pet Rock; Christmas 1975: over a million sold
Hebrew tsur — rock; a title of God (Deu 32:31; Psa 18:2)
Greek petra — "that Rock was Christ" (1Co 10:4)
usage: "Grandpa still has his pet rock. He says it’s the best-behaved pet he ever owned."
Woe unto him that saith to the dumb stone, Arise, it shall teach! (Hab 2:19).
That Rock was Christ (1Co 10:4).

etymology: Invented by the British accountant Edward Craven Walker, who marketed it in 1963 as the "Astro Lamp"; American rights were sold in 1965 and it was sold in the United States as the Lava Lite. A lamp heats a blob of colored wax in a glass bottle of liquid, and the wax rises, cools, and falls in slow, shifting shapes. It became an icon of 1960s–70s psychedelic décor, revived in the 1990s.
biblical_def: A lava lamp is a glass bottle of colored wax that rises and falls in slow, hypnotic blobs when the lamp beneath it warms up. In the late 1960s it was the perfect accessory for a darkened room, a stereo, and an altered state of mind; to this day it says "1970s bedroom." The Christian observation: the lava lamp is a lamp that does not really give light. It glows, but you cannot read by it; it is made to be stared at, not to see by. That is a fair picture of much that the 1960s offered as illumination — mesmerizing, colorful, and useless for finding one’s way. Scripture’s lamps are different. "Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path" (Psa 119:105) — a lamp for walking, not for staring. The Lord Jesus said, "I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life" (Joh 8:12). And He gave His people the duty of being lamps themselves: "Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick; and it giveth light unto all that are in the house. Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven" (Mat 5:15–16). A lamp that only entertains is a lava lamp. A Christian home should have a better one burning: the Word on the table, open, read, and obeyed.
webster_summary: 1960s–70s décor icon (Craven Walker’s Astro Lamp, 1963; US Lava Lite, 1965) whose rising wax mesmerizes but does not illuminate — a foil for the Word that is a lamp unto my feet (Psa 119:105).
webster_full: LAVA LAMP, n. (1960s–70s; Boomer era) A decorative lamp containing colored wax in a liquid-filled glass vessel; heat from the bulb makes the wax rise and fall in slowly changing shapes. Trademark Lava Lite (US).

Webster (1828) — LAVA, noun [probably from flowing, and from the root of Latin fluo, or lavo.] 1. A mass or stream of melted minerals or stony matter which bursts or is thrown from the mouth or sides of a volcano, and is sometimes ejected in such quantities as to overwhelm cities. Catana, at the foot of Etna, has often been destroyed by it, and in 1783, a vast tract of land in Iceland was overspread by an eruption of lava from mount Hecla. 2. The same matter when cool and hardened.
Decode for families: lava lamps are fine on a shelf. The question is what lamp you read by.
scriptures: NUN. Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path.
Joh 8:12
Then spake Jesus again unto them, saying, I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life.
Mat 5:15
Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick; and it giveth light unto all that are in the house.
Mat 5:16
Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven.
The spirit of man is the candle of the LORD, searching all the inward parts of the belly.
corruption_summary: The lava lamp is a lamp made for staring rather than seeing, emblem of a decade that mistook mesmerism for illumination; Scripture’s lamp is the Word, given to walk by.
corruption_paragraphs: The lava lamp belongs to the psychedelic room: dim light, swirling color, music, and a mind drifting. Its appeal was hypnotic, and hypnosis was what many young people of the era were seeking — a way to switch off the analytical mind and float. Scripture never asks the believer to switch off the mind. It asks him to walk in the light, which means seeing clearly enough to put one foot in front of the other in obedience (Psa 119:105).

The lamp is one of Scripture’s favorite images. The spirit of man is "the candle of the LORD" (Pro 20:27); the virgins’ lamps must be trimmed and full; the church is a lampstand. Each image is about usefulness and readiness, not decoration. A lava lamp on a teenager’s dresser is harmless. A soul that is only a lava lamp — glowing, shifting, beautiful, and lighting nothing — is the danger.
roots_summary: Latin labes (a falling) → Italian (Neapolitan) lava (a stream of molten rock) + Greek lampas (a torch) → lamp → 1963 Astro Lamp, 1965 Lava Lite.
roots_lines: Neapolitan Italian lava — a stream (of rain, then of molten rock from Vesuvius)
Greek lampas — a torch → Latin lampas → English lamp
1963: Edward Craven Walker’s Astro Lamp (UK)
1965: American rights sold; marketed as the Lava Lite
Hebrew ner — lamp (Psa 119:105; Pro 20:27)
usage: "Grandpa’s lava lamp still works. He says it takes forty minutes to warm up, like him."
Thy word is a lamp unto my feet (Psa 119:105).
Let your light so shine before men (Mat 5:16).

etymology: Short for eight-track tape (Stereo 8), an endless-loop magnetic tape cartridge with eight parallel tracks (four stereo programs), developed by a consortium led by Bill Lear of Lear Jet in 1964 and offered in Ford cars from the 1966 model year. It dominated car audio in the late 1960s and 1970s — famous for clunking between programs in the middle of a song — and was overtaken by the compact cassette by about 1980.
biblical_def: The 8-track was the tape cartridge Boomers played in their cars in 1970: a plastic brick that slid into the dashboard, played in a continuous loop, and clicked loudly from one track to the next, sometimes in the middle of a song. It was the height of technology and is now a museum piece. The Christian observation: the 8-track teaches two lessons. The first is about obsolescence. Every Boomer owned a box of tapes that became unplayable within ten years. The technology we trust most dates fastest. Against that, Scripture sets the Word that does not date: "Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever" (Heb 13:8); "the word of our God shall stand for ever" (Isa 40:8). The second is about the loop. An 8-track had no rewind; it simply played the same programs over and over until you pulled it out, and people memorized whole albums that way — including where the click came. Scripture commends that kind of repetition with better material: "Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee" (Psa 119:11); "Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly" (Col 3:16); "thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them" (Deu 6:7). Whatever plays on a loop in a mind shapes it. A grandparent who can still sing every song from his 8-track of Abbey Road knows that repetition works. The question is what we put on the loop.
webster_summary: 1960s–70s car-audio tape cartridge (Lear Stereo 8, 1964) that played on an endless loop and was obsolete by about 1980 — a lesson in fading technology beside the Word that stands for ever (Heb 13:8), and in the power of repetition (Psa 119:11).
webster_full: 8-TRACK, n. (1960s–70s; Boomer era) An eight-track tape cartridge: an endless-loop magnetic tape with four stereo programs, played chiefly in car stereos; also the player. Superseded by the cassette c. 1980.

Webster (1828) — TRACK, noun 1. A mark left by something that has passed along; as the track of a ship, a wake; the track of a meteor; the track of a sled or sleigh. 2. A mark or impression left by the foot, either of man or beast. Savages are said to be wonderfully sagacious in finding the tracks of men in the forest.
Decode for families: every generation has its 8-track. Yours is in your pocket.
scriptures: Heb 13:8
Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever.
Isa 40:8
The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.
Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee.
Col 3:16
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.
Deu 6:7
And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.
corruption_summary: A harmless technology; its lessons are the speed with which trusted tools become obsolete, and the power of whatever plays on a loop in the mind.
corruption_paragraphs: Nothing about the 8-track is sinful. But it is a fine object lesson for a technological age. The Boomers trusted it, built their cars around it, and threw it away within a decade. Their grandchildren have watched the same thing happen to CDs, MP3 players, and apps. Each new device feels permanent, and each is gone. The Christian holds technology loosely, because "the fashion of this world passeth away," and holds the Word tightly, because it does not.

The loop is the deeper lesson. What plays repeatedly in a mind becomes the mind’s furniture. The 8-track generation could sing the lyrics of hundreds of songs, many of them foolish or worse. Psalm 119:11 and Deut 6:7 ask for the same repetition with the Word of God. A family that sings psalms and hymns in the car, and memorizes Scripture together, is using the oldest technology there is: the human memory, loaded with truth.
roots_summary: Middle French trac (a trace, a track) → English track → magnetic tape track → 1964 Lear Stereo 8 → 8-track.
roots_lines: Middle French trac — a trace, a footprint; English track — a mark left by passing (1828)
20th c.: a track on magnetic tape or a record
1964: Bill Lear’s consortium develops the Stereo 8 cartridge
1966 model year: offered in Ford cars; dominant in car audio into the 1970s
c. 1980: displaced by the compact cassette
usage: "Grandpa still has a shoebox of 8-tracks and no way to play them. He says it keeps him humble."
Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever (Heb 13:8).
Thy word have I hid in mine heart (Psa 119:11).

etymology: From Ambrose Everett Burnside (1824–1881), Union general, later governor of Rhode Island and U.S. senator, famous for the bushy whiskers that ran down his cheeks into his mustache with a shaved chin. His style was called burnsides by the 1870s; the syllables were reversed into sideburns by the late 1880s, since they grew on the sides of the face. Long, thick sideburns returned as a Boomer fashion in the 1950s (Elvis) and above all in the late 1960s and 1970s. Burnside commanded the Army of the Potomac at the Battle of Fredericksburg, December 11–15, 1862, a disastrous Union defeat.
biblical_def: Sideburns are the whiskers grown down the sides of a man’s face in front of the ears. Elvis wore them in 1956, and by 1972 every young man who could grow them did, the longer and bushier the better. The Christian observation: a family in Fredericksburg has a special reason to know where the word comes from. It is named for General Ambrose Burnside, whose whiskers were famous and whose most famous battle was fought on our own streets in December 1862. Against his officers’ doubts he sent wave after wave of Union soldiers across open ground against Marye’s Heights, and thousands fell at the stone wall. Our Lord asked a question every commander should ask: "what king, going to make war against another king, sitteth not down first, and consulteth whether he be able with ten thousand to meet him that cometh against him with twenty thousand?" (Luk 14:31). "Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall" (Pro 16:18). As for whiskers themselves, Scripture treats hair as a matter of honor and order without making it the measure of a man. Israel was told, "Ye shall not round the corners of your heads, neither shalt thou mar the corners of thy beard" (Lev 19:27), a command separating God’s people from pagan mourning rites; Paul asks whether nature does not teach that long hair is a shame to a man (1Co 11:14); and Absalom’s magnificent hair (2Sa 14:26) became the snare that caught him. The 1970s made hair a statement of identity. Scripture makes it a matter of modest order, and keeps a man’s glory elsewhere: "The hoary head is a crown of glory, if it be found in the way of righteousness" (Pro 16:31).
webster_summary: Whiskers down the sides of the face, named (by reversal, 1880s) for Gen. Ambrose Burnside, the Union commander defeated at Fredericksburg in December 1862; a Boomer fashion of the 1950s–70s — hair Scripture treats as order and honor, not identity (1Co 11:14; Pro 16:31).
webster_full: SIDEBURNS, n. pl. (1880s; Boomer-era fashion 1950s–70s) Strips of hair grown down the sides of a man’s face in front of the ears. From burnsides, after Gen. Ambrose E. Burnside (1824–1881).
Fredericksburg note: Burnside led the Army of the Potomac in the Battle of Fredericksburg (December 1862); the Union assaults on Marye’s Heights failed with heavy loss.
Decode for families: ask Grandpa for a photo from 1974. The sideburns will be in it.
scriptures: Or what king, going to make war against another king, sitteth not down first, and consulteth whether he be able with ten thousand to meet him that cometh against him with twenty thousand?
Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.
Ye shall not round the corners of your heads, neither shalt thou mar the corners of thy beard.
Doth not even nature itself teach you, that, if a man have long hair, it is a shame unto him?

And when he polled his head, (for it was at every year's end that he polled it: because the hair was heavy on him, therefore he polled it:) he weighed the hair of his head at two hundred shekels after the king's weight.
The hoary head is a crown of glory, if it be found in the way of righteousness.
corruption_summary: The 1970s made hair a badge of identity; Scripture treats it as a matter of modest order and honor, and the word’s namesake — defeated at Fredericksburg — is a sober lesson in counting the cost.
corruption_paragraphs: Hair was one of the great battlegrounds of the generation gap. Fathers who wore crew cuts were scandalized by sons with long hair, long sideburns, and beards, and many churches made hair length a test of fellowship. Scripture does speak to hair (1Co 11:14), but it does not make it the center of the Christian life, and churches that did so often drove young people away over inches while neglecting weightier matters. The opposite error was just as real: young men made their hair a declaration of rebellion and identity, which is to make an idol of one’s own head.

The word’s namesake supplies the deeper lesson. Burnside was by most accounts a modest man who did not want high command, and he accepted blame for Fredericksburg afterward. But the battle remains a monument to what happens when a plan is pressed past the point of wisdom. Every Fredericksburg father can walk his son along the stone wall at Marye’s Heights and teach Luk 14:31 — count the cost before the battle — and Pro 16:31 — the only hair that is a crown is the gray head found in the way of righteousness.
roots_summary: Gen. Ambrose E. Burnside (1824–1881) → burnsides (1870s, his whisker style) → reversed to sideburns (late 1880s) → Boomer fashion (1950s–70s).
roots_lines: Ambrose Everett Burnside (1824–1881): Union general, governor of Rhode Island, U.S. senator
December 11–15, 1862: Battle of Fredericksburg; Burnside’s assaults on Marye’s Heights repulsed
1870s: burnsides — whiskers worn in his style
Late 1880s: reversed to sideburns
1950s–70s: Elvis; then long sideburns as a general Boomer style
usage: "Grandpa’s sideburns in 1975 were named after a general who lost a battle three miles from our house."
Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall (Pro 16:18).
The hoary head is a crown of glory, if it be found in the way of righteousness (Pro 16:31).

etymology: Platform (Middle French plate-forme, a flat form or raised level surface) + shoes. Shoes with a thick sole under the whole foot are ancient (the Greek tragic actor’s kothornos, the Venetian chopine of the 1500s), but platform shoes as a mass fashion for both men and women belong to the early-to-mid 1970s — glam rock stars such as Elton John and KISS, disco dancers, and teenagers everywhere teetered on soles several inches thick.
biblical_def: Platform shoes were the towering, thick-soled shoes and boots of the 1970s: men and women alike adding three, four, or six inches to their height, stars stomping across stages, teenagers wobbling to school. The Christian observation: the shoe is a joke about the oldest human wish — to be taller than we are. Our Lord made the same joke gently: "Which of you by taking thought can add one cubit unto his stature?" (Mat 6:27). The platform shoe was a way to add a few inches by money rather than thought, and it changed nothing that mattered. Scripture records a short man who handled his height better. Zacchaeus "sought to see Jesus who he was; and could not for the press, because he was little of stature" (Luk 19:3); so he climbed a sycamore tree, forgot his dignity, and was met by the Lord. The lesson is that God is not impressed by elevation. "Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, let not the rich man glory in his riches: But let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me" (Jer 9:23–24). The glam stars on their platforms were displaying themselves; Zacchaeus up his tree was seeking Christ. Same impulse to get higher, opposite direction. A short boy needs to hear that God measured Saul’s height and chose David’s heart.
webster_summary: 1970s fashion (glam rock and disco) for shoes with thick soles several inches high — an old human wish to be taller that Our Lord gently mocked (Mat 6:27), set against Zacchaeus, little of stature, who climbed a tree to see Jesus (Luk 19:3).
webster_full: PLATFORM SHOES, n. pl. (1970s; Boomer era) Shoes or boots with very thick soles, often several inches high, worn by both sexes. Also platforms.

Webster (1828) — PLATFORM, noun [plat, flat, form.] The sketch of any thing horizontally delineated; the ichnography. 1. A place laid out after any model. 2. In the military art, an elevation of earth or a floor of wood or stone, on which cannons are mounted to fire on an enemy.
Decode for families: platforms come back every twenty years. So does the wish behind them.
scriptures: Mat 6:27
Which of you by taking thought can add one cubit unto his stature?
Luk 19:3
And he sought to see Jesus who he was; and could not for the press, because he was little of stature.
Jer 9:23
Thus saith the LORD, Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, let not the rich man glory in his riches:
Jer 9:24

But let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me, that I am the LORD which exercise lovingkindness, judgment, and righteousness, in the earth: for in these things I delight, saith the LORD.

But the LORD said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.
corruption_summary: Platform shoes bought stature with money and turned height into display; Scripture mocks the effort to add a cubit and shows a short man seeking Christ, not elevation.
corruption_paragraphs: The platform shoe was vanity with a sense of humor. Rock stars wore them to tower over the crowd; ordinary people wore them to be noticed. Nobody was fooled about anyone’s real height. The comedy is the comedy of all self-elevation: everyone can see the soles. Jeremiah’s list of false glories — wisdom, might, riches — could have included inches (Jer 9:23).

The gospel does not make short men tall; it makes small men great. Zacchaeus was a small man in every sense — short, despised, a tax collector — and Christ stopped under his tree and called him by name. The God who "looketh on the heart" (1Sa 16:7) does not need anyone to stand on a platform to be seen.
roots_summary: Middle French plate-forme (a flat form, a ground plan) → English platform (a raised flat surface) + shoes → 1970s platform shoes.
roots_lines: Middle French plate-forme — a plan, a flat surface; Old French plat, flat
Greek kothornos — the high-soled boot of tragic actors
16th c. Venice: chopines, platform overshoes several inches high
Early-to-mid 1970s: glam rock and disco make platform shoes a mass fashion
Greek hēlikia — stature (Mat 6:27; Luk 19:3)
usage: "Grandpa claims he was six foot two in 1974. Grandma says that included four inches of platform."
Which of you by taking thought can add one cubit unto his stature? (Mat 6:27).
He was little of stature (Luk 19:3) — so he climbed a tree to see Jesus.

etymology: Tie + dye: a resist-dyeing technique in which cloth is tied, twisted, or bound before dyeing so that the bound areas resist the color, producing rings, spirals, and bursts. The method is ancient — Japanese shibori, Indian bandhani, West African resist cloth — but the English name is mid-twentieth century, and tie-dyed T-shirts in swirling rainbow colors became a signature of the late-1960s hippie movement, Woodstock, and the Grateful Dead.
biblical_def: Tie-dye is the swirling, many-colored cloth made by binding a shirt with string and dipping it in dye: the uniform of Woodstock, the Grateful Dead, and every summer-camp craft table since. The Christian observation: color in clothing is a biblical delight, and the tie-dye shirt can be enjoyed without apology. Jacob gave Joseph "a coat of many colours" (Gen 37:3) as a sign of love. The high priest’s garments were woven of gold, blue, purple, and scarlet. Lydia, "a seller of purple," was the first convert in Europe, "whose heart the Lord opened" (Act 16:14). God made a world full of color, and a child with a rainbow shirt is enjoying His world. But dye is also one of Scripture’s great images of sin and cleansing. Cloth once dyed is hard to make white again, and so is the soul: "Come now, and let us reason together, saith the LORD: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool" (Isa 1:18). And the clothing of the saints at the end is not tie-dye but white: "to her was granted that she should be arrayed in fine linen, clean and white: for the fine linen is the righteousness of saints" (Rev 19:8). The hippies tie-dyed their shirts to proclaim a new age; the gospel washes the soul white to prepare it for the new heavens and earth. A family can make tie-dye shirts on a summer afternoon and talk about Isaiah 1:18 while the colors set.
webster_summary: Ancient resist-dyeing technique, named in the mid-20th century, whose swirling rainbow T-shirts became the hippie uniform of the late 1960s — a delight in color Scripture shares (Gen 37:3) and an image of the stained soul made white (Isa 1:18).
webster_full: TIE-DYE, n. (mid-20th c.; Boomer era fashion, late 1960s–) A method of hand-dyeing fabric by tying portions tightly so they resist the dye, producing irregular patterns; a garment so dyed. v.t. To dye by this method.

Webster (1828) — DYE, verb transitive [Latin tingo, for tigo.] To stain; to color; to give a new and permanent color to; applied particularly to cloth or the materials of cloth, as wool, cotton, silk and linen; also to hats, leather, etc. It usually expresses more or a deeper color than tinge.
Decode for families: tie-dye is one of the few Boomer fashions with no expiration date. Enjoy it.
scriptures: Gen 37:3
Now Israel loved Joseph more than all his children, because he was the son of his old age: and he made him a coat of many colours.
And a certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple, of the city of Thyatira, which worshipped God, heard us: whose heart the Lord opened, that she attended unto the things which were spoken of Paul.
Isa 1:18
Come now, and let us reason together, saith the LORD: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool.
Rev 19:8
And to her was granted that she should be arrayed in fine linen, clean and white: for the fine linen is the righteousness of saints.
corruption_summary: Tie-dye is a cheerful craft that the counterculture made a uniform of its new age; Scripture delights in color and uses dye as the image of sin that only God can wash white.
corruption_paragraphs: There is little to correct in tie-dye itself. It is a folk craft, cheap and joyful, and children love it. Its association with the drug culture of the late 1960s — the swirling patterns were meant to evoke an acid trip — is a matter of history rather than of the cloth. Paul’s principle covers it: "Every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving."

The deeper use of the image is Isaiah’s. Scarlet dye was the most permanent color known to the ancient world; it would not wash out. God’s promise in Isa 1:18 is the promise to do the impossible — to make the dyed soul white. The saints of Revelation are clothed in white linen, which is "the righteousness of saints" (Rev 19:8), given to them, not earned.
roots_summary: Old English tígan (to tie) + Old English déagian (to dye) → mid-20th-c. tie-dye → late-1960s hippie fashion.
roots_lines: Old English tígan — to bind; déagian — to color, to dye
Ancient resist dyeing: Japanese shibori, Indian bandhani, West African resist cloth
Mid-20th c.: the English term tie-dye
Late 1960s: tie-dyed T-shirts become a hippie signature (Woodstock, 1969)
Hebrew shani — scarlet; tola — crimson (Isa 1:18)
usage: "We made tie-dye shirts at Grandpa’s. He said the last time he did it was 1969 and it was not at church camp."
He made him a coat of many colours (Gen 37:3).
Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow (Isa 1:18).

etymology: Two signs share the name. The peace symbol — a circle enclosing a vertical line and two lines angled downward — was designed in February 1958 by the British artist Gerald Holtom for a march against nuclear weapons, combining the semaphore signals for N and D ("nuclear disarmament"); it was adopted by the Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament and spread to the American civil-rights and anti-Vietnam movements in the 1960s. The peace sign gesture — two fingers raised in a V — was Winston Churchill’s "V for Victory" in 1941, re-read as "peace" by the 1960s counterculture.
biblical_def: The peace sign is both a gesture — two fingers in a V — and a symbol — the circle with the downward lines — and to Boomers it meant the whole anti-war, anti-nuke, love-and-peace hope of the 1960s. Grandchildren still flash it in photos without a thought. The Christian observation: the sign promised peace and could not give it; Scripture names the One who can. The gesture began as Churchill’s V for victory in a war against real evil, and the 1960s turned it into a plea for peace by disarmament. Both are signs pointing at something beyond themselves. Scripture’s sign of peace is a Person: "For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given ... and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace" (Isa 9:6). His peace is a different kind: "Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you" (Joh 14:27). It is first peace with God, "Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ" (Rom 5:1), and then peace between enemies: "For he is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us" (Eph 2:14). And it was made at a cost the 1960s never reckoned with: "having made peace through the blood of his cross" (Col 1:20). The Christian’s peace sign is the cross. A child who flashes two fingers for a photo is not sinning; but his parents can show him the sign that actually delivers what it promises.
webster_summary: Boomer emblem of 1960s peace and disarmament — Holtom’s 1958 nuclear-disarmament symbol and Churchill’s V gesture re-read as "peace" — a sign of a hope Scripture fulfils only in the Prince of Peace, who made peace through the blood of His cross (Col 1:20).
webster_full: PEACE SIGN, n. (Boomer era, 1960s–) 1. A hand gesture with the index and middle fingers raised in a V, palm outward, signifying peace (earlier, Churchill’s "V for Victory," 1941). 2. The peace symbol, a circle enclosing a vertical stroke and two downward diagonals, designed by Gerald Holtom (1958) for the nuclear-disarmament movement.

Webster (1828) — SIGN, noun [Latin signum; Gr. deicnumt.] 1. A token; something by which another thing is shown or represented; any visible thing, any motion, appearance or event which indicates the existence or approach of something else. Thus we speak of signs of fair weather or of a storm, and of external marks which are signs of a good constitution. 2. A motion, action, nod or gesture indicating a wish or command. They made signs to his father, how he would have him called. Luke 1:62 . 3. A wonder; a miracle; a prodigy; a remarkable transaction, event or phenomenon. Through mighty signs and wonders. Romans 15:19 . Luke 1:62 1.
Decode for families: in a selfie, two fingers usually mean "hi." Tell your children what it meant in 1968, and what the cross means always.
scriptures: Isa 9:6

For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder: and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace.
Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid.
Rom 5:1
Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ:
Eph 2:14
For he is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us;
Col 1:20
And, having made peace through the blood of his cross, by him to reconcile all things unto himself; by him, I say, whether they be things in earth, or things in heaven.
corruption_summary: The peace sign stood for a peace sought by protest and disarmament; Scripture offers a peace that is a Person, made first between God and man through the blood of the cross.
corruption_paragraphs: Symbols carry hopes, and the peace sign carried a generation’s hope that war could be ended by refusing to fight. The hope was sincere and the fear of nuclear war was rational. But the peace movement’s peace had no account of why men fight, and so no cure for it. James had already given the diagnosis: wars come from the lusts that war in our members. A sign on a placard cannot reach that far down.

The gospel’s peace begins at the root. It reconciles the sinner to God (Rom 5:1), and only then reconciles enemies to each other (Eph 2:14). The world gives peace by treaty and slogan; Christ gives it "not as the world giveth" (Joh 14:27) — by His own death. That is why the church’s symbol is not a circle with lines but a cross.
roots_summary: Latin pax + Latin signum (a mark, a token) → 1941 Churchill’s V sign → 1958 Holtom’s peace symbol (semaphore N + D) → 1960s counterculture peace sign.
roots_lines: Latin pax — peace; signum — a mark, token, standard
1941: Winston Churchill popularizes the V-for-Victory gesture
February 1958: Gerald Holtom designs the nuclear-disarmament symbol (semaphore N and D)
Easter 1958: first carried on the march to Aldermaston, England
1960s: adopted by the American anti-war movement and counterculture
usage: "Grandma flashes a peace sign in every photo. She says she means Joh 14:27 now."
His name shall be called ... The Prince of Peace (Isa 9:6).
Having made peace through the blood of his cross (Col 1:20).

etymology: Love + beads (Old English gebed, a prayer — from the counting of prayers on a string, whence bead for any small pierced ball). Love beads, strings of colorful glass or wooden beads worn by hippies of both sexes as a token of peace and love, often handmade and exchanged as gifts, were a fashion of 1967–70; they drew partly on Eastern prayer beads (the Hindu and Buddhist mala) that came into the counterculture with Hare Krishna and Transcendental Meditation.
biblical_def: Love beads were the hippie’s necklace: strands of bright beads worn by young men and women alike as a badge of peace and love, sometimes exchanged as gifts, sometimes borrowed from Eastern prayer practice. The Christian observation: the word bead itself once meant a prayer — the old English gebed — because beads were used to count prayers. Love beads took the form and emptied it, or filled it with Eastern mysticism. Scripture has a great deal to say about ornaments around the neck, and it points them toward wisdom and truth. "For they shall be an ornament of grace unto thy head, and chains about thy neck" (Pro 1:9) — said of a father’s instruction and a mother’s law. "Let not mercy and truth forsake thee: bind them about thy neck; write them upon the table of thine heart" (Pro 3:3). Scripture also knows how ornaments can go wrong. Isaiah’s daughters of Zion wore "tinkling ornaments ... The chains, and the bracelets" (Isa 3:18–19) to display their pride, and Aaron melted down Israel’s earrings to make the golden calf (Exo 32:2). And Peter tells believers not to make outward adorning their glory but "the hidden man of the heart" (1Pe 3:4). A string of beads is no sin. But the best love beads a child can wear are the ones Proverbs describes: a father’s wisdom and a mother’s law, mercy and truth, bound about the neck and written on the heart.
webster_summary: Hippie necklaces (1967–70) of colorful beads worn as tokens of peace and love, partly borrowed from Eastern prayer beads — Scripture’s better necklace is mercy and truth bound about the neck (Pro 3:3) and a parent’s instruction as chains of grace (Pro 1:9).
webster_full: LOVE BEADS, n. pl. (Boomer slang, 1967–70) Strings of colorful beads worn, especially by hippies, as a symbol of peace and love; often handmade and given as gifts.

Webster (1828) — BEAD, noun 1. A little perforated ball, to be strung on a thread, and worn about the neck, for ornament. A string of beads is called a necklace. Beads are made of gold, pearl, amber, steel, garnet, coral, diamond, crystal, pastes, glasses, etc. The Romanists use strings of beads in rehearsing their prayers. Hence the phrase, to tell beads, and to be at one’s beads, is to be at prayer. 2. Any small globular body; hence the glass globules, used in traffic with savages, and sold in strings, are called beads; also a bubble on spirit. 3. In architecture, a round molding, commonly made upon the edge of a piece of stuff, in the Corinthian and Roman orders, cut or carved in short embossments, like beads in necklaces.of beads, is a charge given by a priest to his parishioners, to repeat certain pater-nosters upon their beads for a departed soul.
Decode for families: bead once meant "prayer." Ask what your child’s bracelets are for.
scriptures: Pro 1:9
For they shall be an ornament of grace unto thy head, and chains about thy neck.
Pro 3:3
Let not mercy and truth forsake thee: bind them about thy neck; write them upon the table of thine heart:
Isa 3:18
In that day the Lord will take away the bravery of their tinkling ornaments about their feet, and their cauls, and their round tires like the moon,
Isa 3:19
The chains, and the bracelets, and the mufflers,
Exo 32:2
And Aaron said unto them, Break off the golden earrings, which are in the ears of your wives, of your sons, and of your daughters, and bring them unto me.
But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.
corruption_summary: Love beads borrowed the form of prayer beads and filled it with sentiment or Eastern mysticism; Scripture binds mercy and truth about the neck and warns of ornaments that serve pride or idols.
corruption_paragraphs: The love bead was a gentle fashion with a religious shadow. Many hippies wore beads borrowed from Hindu and Buddhist practice, and the counterculture’s turn east — Hare Krishna, Transcendental Meditation, the Beatles in India in 1968 — brought prayer beads into American wardrobes stripped of their meaning or loaded with another. Every generation has its version; today it may be crystal bracelets for "energy" or charm bracelets for luck. The Christian asks of any ornament: what is it for?

Proverbs answers with a beautiful image. The best necklace a young person can wear is the instruction of godly parents (Pro 1:9), and mercy and truth bound about the neck (Pro 3:3). Those beads do not break or fade, and they are visible in every conversation.
roots_summary: Old English gebed (a prayer) → Middle English bede (a prayer; a prayer-bead) → bead (any small pierced ball) + love → 1967–70 love beads.
roots_lines: Old English gebed — a prayer; biddan — to pray, to ask
Middle English bede — a prayer; the small balls on which prayers were counted
English bead — any small perforated ball strung for ornament (1828)
1967–70: love beads — hippie necklaces; Eastern mala influence
Hebrew anaq — to put on as a necklace; chains about the neck (Pro 1:9)
usage: "Grandma traded love beads with a girl at a 1969 concert. She found her again forty years later at a Bible study."
Bind them about thy neck; write them upon the table of thine heart (Pro 3:3).
An ornament of grace unto thy head, and chains about thy neck (Pro 1:9).

etymology: The Woodstock Music and Art Fair, billed as "3 Days of Peace & Music," held August 15–18, 1969, on Max Yasgur’s dairy farm in Bethel, New York — about forty miles from the town of Woodstock that gave it its name. Roughly 400,000 people came; rain turned the field to mud; food and sanitation failed; and Jimi Hendrix played "The Star-Spangled Banner" in the closing set on Monday morning. Joni Mitchell’s song "Woodstock" (1970) sang of getting "back to the garden." The name became shorthand for the whole counterculture: "the Woodstock generation."
biblical_def: Woodstock is the festival of August 1969 — three days, nearly half a million young people, rain, mud, music, drugs, nudity, and a remarkable peace — and it became the name for the whole Boomer counterculture. "He’s a Woodstock kid." The Christian observation: Woodstock’s anthem said the quiet part out loud. The young people of 1969 believed they had to "get back to the garden" — to recover an Eden of innocence, nature, and love. Scripture agrees that we were made for a garden and lost it, and it explains why the gate cannot be opened from our side: "So he drove out the man; and he placed at the east of the garden of Eden Cherubims, and a flaming sword which turned every way, to keep the way of the tree of life" (Gen 3:24). Woodstock tried to walk back in on music and marijuana, and found mud. The Babel-builders had a similar plan: "let us make us a name" (Gen 11:4) — a city built by human unity. John’s summary fits the festival: "the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not of the Father, but is of the world" (1Jn 2:16). Yet the longing was right. The way back to the tree of life has been opened, not by a festival but by a cross, and the Bible ends in a garden-city: "Blessed are they that do his commandments, that they may have right to the tree of life, and may enter in through the gates into the city" (Rev 22:14). A grandparent who was there in the mud can be told: you were right that we need to get back to the garden. There is only one Gate.
webster_summary: The festival of August 15–18, 1969 (Bethel, NY; about 400,000 attending) and shorthand for the Boomer counterculture — whose anthem longed to get "back to the garden," a gate Scripture says only Christ reopens (Gen 3:24; Rev 22:14).
webster_full: WOODSTOCK, n. (proper; 1969) The Woodstock Music and Art Fair, August 15–18, 1969, Bethel, New York; by extension the late-1960s counterculture as a whole. Woodstock generation, Woodstock Nation.
Decode for families: about 400,000 attended; millions now remember being there. Ask your grandparents gently.
scriptures: Gen 3:24
So he drove out the man; and he placed at the east of the garden of Eden Cherubims, and a flaming sword which turned every way, to keep the way of the tree of life.
Gen 11:4
And they said, Go to, let us build us a city and a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven; and let us make us a name, lest we be scattered abroad upon the face of the whole earth.
For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not of the Father, but is of the world.
Blessed are they that do his commandments, that they may have right to the tree of life, and may enter in through the gates into the city.
Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching.
corruption_summary: Woodstock sought a return to Eden through music, drugs, and human unity; Scripture shows the garden’s gate guarded by a flaming sword and opened only by Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: Woodstock has been mythologized more than any event of its era: half a million young people in peace, sharing food, helping strangers, enduring rain together. Some of that was true and admirable. But the myth leaves out the overdoses, the medical tents, the exploitation, and the fact that four months later the Altamont concert in California ended in violence and death. The garden could not be reached by the road they took. Babel teaches the same lesson: human unity without God builds a tower, not a gate (Gen 11:4).

The longing itself deserves honor. Joni Mitchell’s line about getting back to the garden names the deepest ache of every human heart, and Scripture shares it. The church, too, is a great gathering of the young and old who have left the world to come together — "not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together" (Heb 10:25) — and its gathering points to the true garden-city at the end of the Bible, where the tree of life stands open to those washed in the blood of the Lamb (Rev 22:14).
roots_summary: Old English wudu (wood) + stoc (a place) → Woodstock, New York (an artists’ town) → August 1969 festival (held at Bethel) → byword for the counterculture.
roots_lines: Old English wudu — wood, forest; stoc — a place, an outlying farm
Woodstock, New York — a Catskills artists’ colony that lent the festival its name
August 15–18, 1969: festival held on Max Yasgur’s farm, Bethel, NY
1970: Joni Mitchell’s "Woodstock" ("back to the garden"); the documentary film
December 1969: the Altamont concert, often called the counterculture’s end
usage: "Grandpa was at Woodstock for one day. He says it rained, he lost a shoe, and he called home."
To keep the way of the tree of life (Gen 3:24).
That they may have right to the tree of life (Rev 22:14).
